page: Google Cloud Platform n1-highcpu-2 is an x86_64 architecture virtual machine belonging to the n1 server family. It features 2 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 1 physical Intel Xeon core operating at 2.3 GHz, with hyper-threading enabled. The system is equipped with 2.0 GB of system memory, yielding a low memory-to-core ratio of 0.9 GB per vCPU. It does not include bundled local storage or integrated GPU hardware, and provides zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark evaluations place this instance in the lower performance tiers. The stress-ng single-core CPU performance score of 1086.39 is categorized as weak, while the multi-core score of 1408.88 falls into the bottom 10%. Memory bandwidth is similarly constrained, with read-only large block speeds at 13.22 GB/sec and write speeds at 11.3 GB/sec. Cryptographic and compression tasks also reflect these limitations, with a single-threaded gzip compression speed of 18.91 GB/sec and a Passmark CPU score of 1638.85.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the n1-highcpu-2 offers a low-cost entry point for compute-bound tasks that do not require substantial memory footprints. However, the low resource density and poor benchmark-per-resource tradeoffs make it unsuitable for memory-intensive databases or high-throughput applications. It is best suited for lightweight background workers, basic web serving with low concurrency, simple scripting, and small-scale development or testing environments.
description: Google Cloud Platform n1-highcpu-2 is an x86_64 virtual machine from the n1 family, configured with 2 dedicated vCPUs and 2.0 GB of RAM. Powered by an Intel Xeon processor running at 2.3 GHz, this instance features 1 physical core with hyper-threading, 45 MB of L3 cache, and lacks local storage or GPU accelerators. Performance benchmarks indicate an entry-level profile, with stress-ng single-core and multi-core scores falling into the lower percentiles, and memory bandwidth limited to 13.22 GB/sec for large block reads. Qualitatively, this server represents a budget-friendly option for compute-centric workloads with minimal memory requirements. It is best utilized for lightweight background tasks, basic web serving, and development environments rather than high-throughput database or data-processing applications.
